utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And I'll address the new Prosecution team and ask the Prosecution for their appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Tecla Henry-Benjamin, Daryl Mundis, our case manager, Hasan Younis, and I should note, Mr. President, that later this morning our case manager will substitute and Mr. Andres Vatter will be with us later this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And the appearances for the Defence. They're all present.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel, Stephane Bourgon, our co-counsel, and Mirna Milanovic, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present, members of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, and everyone else in this courtroom. We'll be continuing with the hearing of a witness today, but before we do so, the Trial Chamber would like to provide information -- would like to provide the parties with some information concerning the following matter. The Trial Chamber has taken note of the letter of the Prosecution dated 19th of May, 2004 in which the Prosecution said that they no longer wanted to call 19 witnesses included in their witness list. These are numbers 1, 2, 5, 30, 35, 38, 51, 58, 63, 77, 78, 85, 93, 98, 123, 125, 135, 136, and 139. These are the witnesses on the list. The Trial Chamber deliberated about the matter yesterday and would like to know whether it is necessary for the Trial Chamber, pursuant to Rule 98 and in the interests of justice, to call a number of these witnesses to appear before the Trial Chamber immediately after the Prosecution has presented its case. As an example, the Trial Chamber would call witnesses 1, 2, 38, 77, 85, 123, 135, 136, and 139. But before we reach a decision, the Trial Chamber would like to invite both parties to state their position, to express their opinion about this measure that the Trial Chamber is considering. This could be done either today or tomorrow. If the Prosecution could inform us of its position now, they could do so today. But if they need time to reflect, they could do so tomorrow. Naturally, I will also give the floor to the Defence. Following the comments made by both parties, the Trial Chamber will reach its final decision as soon as possible. I will now turn to Mr. Mundis. You've heard what I have just said. Would you like to express your opinion today, or would you prefer to think about the matter before you tell us about what your opinion is?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution would prefer to express its views on this matter tomorrow. We will do so orally, if that's acceptable to the Chamber, in order to save time. I do have two matters of clarification that perhaps Your Honours could help us with prior to the Prosecution setting forth its view. First, whether the nine witnesses that Your Honour just mentioned as an example would be the only nine witnesses, so that I could limit my comments to those witnesses, or if those were simply examples and that the Trial Chamber might be contemplating additional witnesses. That would be my first area that I would seek some guidance on. Second of all, Mr. President, clearly Rule 98 permits the Chamber to call witnesses, and of course Rule 85, setting forth the presentation of evidence, permits the Chamber to vary the order of the presentation of cases in the interests of justice, as Your Honour has just indicated. I do think it might be helpful to the parties, however, to get some type of clarification in the event the Chamber - again, in the interests of justice - pursuant to the preambular language of Rule 85, could give us some guidance as to the Chamber's position with respect to the anticipated submissions pursuant to Rule 98 bis by the Defence and how the fact that the Chamber might be varying the normal order of the presentation of evidence, how that would impact upon Rule 98 bis submissions. And I raise that, Mr. President, because of course Rule 98 bis indicates that upon the closing of the Prosecution case the Defence shall file their Rule 98 motion, if any - and I assume there will be in this case - seven days after the close of the Prosecution case. And I'm just wondering if perhaps we could get some guidance from the Chamber as to what would be the Chamber's view or how the calling of witnesses, the varying of the order pursuant to Rule 85, would impact upon those Rule 98 bis submissions. For example, if we closed our case in the 10th of June, for example, that would trigger certain obligations under Rule 98 bis, in terms of the filing of those submissions, which, while those submissions are being filed, we may then be in a situation where the Chamber is calling judges [sic] pursuant to Rule 98 and varying the order of the presentation pursuant to Rule 85. And I'm just seeking some clarification or guidance from the Chamber in that respect. I think that might be helpful to all the parties prior to the parties being given an opportunity to be heard on the issue. I note from the transcript, Mr. President, page 4, line 16, obviously I was making reference to the Chamber calling witnesses and not calling judges. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. As far as the two matters that you would like to be clarified are concerned, I'll immediately address the most important issue, namely the use of Rule 85 and 98 in combination. As you know, Rule 85 provides that each party is entitled to call witnesses and to present evidence. The order is as follows: "evidence for the prosecution"; "evidence for the defence"; "prosecution evidence in rebuttal"; "defence evidence in rejoinder." And then: "evidence ordered by the Trial Chamber pursuant to Rule 98." That's the general rule. But under (A) in 85 the following is stated: "Unless otherwise directed by the Trial Chamber in the interests of justice." So at this point in time, without taking into account Rule 98, the Trial Chamber is thinking of calling the nine witnesses once the Prosecution has presented its case at the conclusion of the first stage, in other words. That means that it would be before the Defence presents its case. If this is the decision that we take, we will take it because it is in the interest of justice. So such is the clarifications I could provide about this issue. As far as a motion for acquittal is concerned, under Rule 98, this is a different matter and we shouldn't confuse these two matters, although the one matter could arise from the other. But nevertheless it's not necessary to establish a direct link between them. At this point in time, 19 witnesses were scheduled. The Prosecution would like to withdraw 19. The Trial Chamber thinks that there are at least 9 witnesses out of these 19 witnesses who should be heard for the sake of -- in the interest of justice. But before we reach this decision, before we take such a decision, the Trial Chamber would like to know what the position of both parties is with regard to this matter, and this is why you will inform us of your position tomorrow, and I will then let the Defence take the floor to address the first issue, the issue of calling nine witnesses. Naturally, if these nine witnesses do appear, this will mean that we'll need additional time for the hearings. According to the provisional schedule, we were to finish with the hearings in mid-June, but you should remember that on a number of occasions the Trial Chamber pointed out that this was a provisional date because as everyone is aware, various matters may arise in the course of proceedings and as a result the provisional dates are not adhered to; in fact, quite frequently an extension of time is required. And this would be the case if nine additional witnesses are called. Naturally, it would be necessary to add to these nine witnesses another witness with regard to whom a decision was taken yesterday. This written decision has been forwarded to the registry, so you will be provided with it. And likewise there is the matter of archivists, whom we would like to call as well. The two or three archivists concerned could come on the same day; they would enable us to proceed more expeditiously. We need a little information from them, so it shouldn't take too long to hear these witnesses. We could deal with the matter quite rapidly. Another issue concerns witnesses who haven't been scheduled to date, and this might arise from the videotapes. This is something that could be a result of the videotapes. So we have scheduled the appearance of a witness on Friday. I would like to ask the Prosecution whether when this witness is called, whether they would like the video to be broadcast. Because certain witnesses have appeared the Prosecution had the possibility of tendering the video through these witnesses, and this wasn't done. So this is a matter that is still pending. The Trial Chamber said that it would be good if the video were broadcast, if the video were shown, and if that's the case, we would call the relevant witnesses for the video. But naturally this is a matter that is not certain. As far as these additional witnesses are concerned, this issue is not certain. So, Mr. Mundis, if you would like to address this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Let me just first mention the archivists, because that was also addressed by Your Honours. If I may propose the following course of -- with respect to the archivists: The Prosecution, again in order to expedite the proceedings, is planning on attempting to adduce the evidence of the archivists via Rule 92 bis and then of course making them available for any additional questions from the Defence or from the Trial Chamber. But our proposal at this stage, Mr. President, with respect to the archivists, is to take statements from them pursuant to Rule 92 bis and in the event there are additional questions, if Your Honours would prefer that we bring them, we can certainly make those efforts. But in order to save time, we were planning on taking statements pursuant to Rule 92 bis. And one of the reasons I say that, Mr. President, is it seems to the Prosecution that as a matter of fairness to the Defence, we need to take written statements from these witnesses anyway, rather than simply calling them without providing the Defence with written witness statements. And in -- since we have to take written witness statements, it would make sense to us to expedite things by taking those pursuant to Rule 92 bis and then making those witnesses available in the event the Defence or Your Honours have additional questions. If that's not the course that the Trial Chamber at this phase wishes us to take, then we will certainly rethink our plan in that respect. With respect to the videos, the witness who's scheduled for Friday has not yet arrived in The Hague. My understanding from discussing this matter with Mr. Withopf is that the witness who is - excuse me - scheduled for Friday has not in fact ever seen the videotape, so it may be problematic to show that videotape to him in court as a means of authenticating that videotape. The witness certainly in the course of his professional duties encountered Mujahedin in Central Bosnia and made reference to interviewing at least one of them. That interview was videotaped, but the Mujahedin videotape that has been discussed throughout these proceedings is not the same videotape that the witness refers to in his statement, at least according to the information that I have right now. I will certainly discuss that with the witness when he does arrive in The Hague and perhaps we are mistaken, but at this point there's no indication to us that this witness has actually seen the videotape in question. We're in the process of trying to gather certain information about the videotapes that are on the consolidated exhibit list in light of the oral order that they be broadcast in public. We're attempting to come up with a precise figure as to precisely how long these tapes are. Some of the tapes are compilations and are rather lengthy, and I will be in a better position to inform the Trial Chamber about the precise amount of time required to publicly broadcast those videotapes in the near future. That's one of the many issues that the Prosecution is working on, in light of the order of the Trial Chamber. And again, we haven't seen the written decision yet, but based on the oral order, we're working on the issues that Mr. President addressed to us earlier this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As far as the application of Rule 92 bis is concerned, with regard to the archivists we'll deliberate about the matter in the course of the afternoon and inform you tomorrow of what we think about your position is. It's true that Rule 92 bis could be useful, but notwithstanding this Rule, it might be required by the Defence to have the witness examined. In such a case, this procedure wouldn't be useful because the witness would have to appear. To call the witness might be a matter of judicial economy, because we wouldn't need to have a preliminary procedure involving written testimony. We'll deliberate about the matter and inform you what our final position is. You also said that as far as the nine witnesses were concerned you'd inform us of your position tomorrow. The Defence should also inform us of their position tomorrow. We'll deal with this matter again at the beginning of the hearing tomorrow. We'll now start with the examination of the witness. Have any protective measures been requested? Ms. Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No protective measures have been requested. Very well. We will call the witness into the courtroom, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I would first like to make sure that you are receiving the interpretation of what I am saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've been called here as a witness for the Prosecution. Before you take the solemn declaration, I would like to ask you to tell me your first and last names and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Ulf Henricsson, and I'm born on the 1st of February, 1942.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which town or village were you born in and what is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm a Swede, and born in Stockholm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm an army officer, working at -- as head of the Department for Leadership at the Swedish National Defence College.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What rank do you hold in the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm a brigadier general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, what was your rank and what duties did you perform in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a colonel and commanded the 1st Nordic Battle Group, NordBat 2, from middle of September until the beginning of April 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified before an international or a national court about the events in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1993 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which tribunal have you already testified before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was here in The Hague, this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could you tell me which case you testified in, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was linked to this event, and that was what happened in the town of Vares a week before the event we will talk about today. And I was here -- I don't remember exactly. I think it was in 1996. It was the case against Ivica Rajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you a witness for the Prosecution or for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please read out the solemn declaration that the usher will show to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. You may sit down now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you have already testified, you are used to the procedure, but I would just like to remind you of the procedure. You have been called here as a witness for the Prosecution, and you will first answer a series of questions put to you by the Prosecution. I assume that Ms. Benjamin, who is to your right behind the transparent lectern, will be answering -- will be conducting the examination-in-chief. Once the Prosecution has completed its examination-in-chief, Defence counsel, who are to your left, will conduct their cross-examination. As you will see, the questions put to you by the Defence will be somewhat different to those put to you by the Prosecution. According to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal, the purpose of the Defence's questions is to verify your credibility and to obtain information on the context. After this initial stage has been completed, after the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination have been completed, the Prosecution may re-examine you. The three Judges sitting before you may also put questions to you. According to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the Judges may ask you questions at any point in time, but as a rule Judges prefer to wait for both parties to conclude their examination before the Judges ask you questions. Once the Judges have asked a witness questions, both parties can ask a witness additional questions in order to clarify some of the answers provided to the Judges. So roughly speaking, this is the procedure that we will be following. In addition, I would like to inform you of two other matters: You have taken the solemn declaration. As a result, false testimony should not be given. And secondly - but this shouldn't apply to you - when a witness answers a question, if the witness's answer could be used against him, the witness may refuse to answer the question. In such a case, which is exceptional, the Judges may compel the witness to answer the question but the witness is granted a form of immunity by the Trial Chamber. So this is a very brief summary I wanted to provide you with in order to ensure that these proceedings and your examination runs smoothly. To the extent that this is possible, try to provide clear and precise answers to the questions. You might be asked questions about events that happened over ten years ago, and your memory may not be quite accurate. If that is the case, do inform the Trial Chamber of the fact. And if you encounter any difficulties, inform us of the fact too because the Judges are here to deal with any difficulties that may arise. It is now 9.35. We'll be working until 10.30, which is when we will have our break. So we have about an hour for the examination-in-chief. Without wasting any more time, I will now let Ms. Benjamin take the floor for her examination-in-chief. Ms. Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Brigadier General. Brigadier, you explained to the Trial Chamber a while ago your rank, present and while you were in Bosnia. Could you briefly give the Trial Chamber an account of your military career, please.

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Yes. I became an officer in 1969 and make a normal troop career during the 1970s and worked at the proper schools, and then I worked as a general staff officer for six years, and then I made a new service as battalion commander. I worked with the Swedish tank programme some years, and then I became brigade commander in 1991 and served as brigade commander in -- from 1991 to 1994, and during that period I served as commanding officer of the Nordic Battle Group down in Bosnia. Then I served as division commander from the Swedish Eastern Division until 1999, and after that I served two years as head of the EC military department in Sarajevo. And since 2002, I'm head of the Department for leadership at the National Defence College.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as commander and leader of the NordBat 2 in Bosnia, could you please tell us what was your role, what was your duty in Bosnia, please.

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: The duty or the task for the battle group was to support the humanitarian aid in our area of responsibility. It was to establish freedom of movement and to try to negotiate a cease-fire in the area and to establish a secure environment. And we were deployed, or my area of responsibility was from the Sava River in the north down to south of Vares, some 100 kilometres, and from the Drina River in the east until a line north-south drawn through Doboj. And it was an area of 5.000 square kilometres, and I had 1.300 soldiers to do the job with, which was more or less a mission impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your period of your tenure in Bosnia, could you tell us when it began and when it ceased, please.

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Well, I came down to Bosnia more or less permanently for this period on -- in the middle of September 1993 and stayed until, I think it was 7th of April, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: On your arrival in Bosnia, could you state for the Trial Chamber your immediate role, what you did and how you started your tenure.

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Could you explain what you mean by this.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: When you got into Bosnia in mid-September --

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: -- could you tell us how you began your tenure, please, what you set out to do.

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: I of course set out to prepare to solve my task. And in September, the two weeks, we -- I travelled around to learn the new area, to meet commanders on different levels, and of course also get convenient with my superior staff or commander in Kiseljak in BH command, and the -- prepare the deployment of the battle group, which started on the 1st of October from Scandinavia and lasted until February 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, how would you describe Vares when you got into your area of responsibility? How would you describe the area?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Well, the Vares area is -- if I start with the town, it's an old mining town deep in a valley, going north to south, very -- and the mining in the town has ceased before the war, and it was a town with a Croat majority. And I think the number of inhabitants was around 15.000 and maybe the majority of the Croat was at least two to three -- two-thirds of the population. And around Vares it was a hilly, mountainous terrain, and it was a very important place, both for military purpose and civilian, because through Vares went the only road -- supply road up to the Tuzla area. And on -- rather close to the road up north went the Serbian lines, both east and west. So it was strategic, very important.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: With respect to units, how many units - and I speak of the Bosnian army now - how many units did you meet in Vares?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Vares was inside the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the Vares area were under the responsibility of the Bobovac Brigade, which was also unique, was a Croat brigade, under the command of a mainly Bosniak corps. And we had -- well, we knew that there were tensions and Vares a hot spot when we came down, and that's why I deployed my first company, the company first coming to the area, in Vares. And we had good cooperation with the Bobovac Brigade and with the mayor of the town, but in -- somewhere around the 20th of October the command or the -- both the Bobovac Brigade and the town was taken over by Croat extremists which was said - and I think that's proved too also - from Kiseljak and Kakanj, under command of a man named Ivica Rajic, a former JNA major, and that changed the situation considerably. So our cooperation vanished and it got -- it became a very tough situation and the Bosniaks was impeded, jailed, and it ended up with a massacre in Stupni Do, which is the other case I referred to earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Would I be correct, Brigadier General, if I were to say, then, that Vares was not a normal situation?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: I would say it was a fairly normal situation in Bosnia at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. You were privy to the first assault somewhere around the end of October. Could you --

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: The first assault from the Croat side, I would say, occurred on the 23rd of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So could you please explain to the Trial Chamber what happened and your role in this.

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Yes. What happened was -- well, the first assault in that area - I'll go back a little - was, I think, on the 21st of October, when the village of Kopjari in the southern part of the Bobovac Brigade area were assaulted and the Croat inhabitants were expelled. It was some killings, and the village was then burnt. And that was on the 21st.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: At this time, did you see it necessary to request more assistance? Did you find it becoming difficult?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Well, I didn't acquire that because there were no assistance to get at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: But things began to get tense; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Then comes the second attack that you have been privy to. And which -- could you tell the Trial Chamber how this would have changed the whole situation in Vares, please.

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Yes. And that was on the 23rd of October, when the Croat extremists made an attack on the village of Stupni Do, which was a Bosniak village some kilometres outside the town of Vares. And we -- and I negotiated with them together with my company commander, and we demanded access to the town -- to the village to see what happened, and we had also at that time communication with the Bosniak army, the federation army, and with the operational group in Dabravine and --

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Commander, if I may interrupt.

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: How did this affect Vares during your tenure?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: It affected Vares on a -- because, of course, the Bosniaks were very afraid and fled the town and we ended up with hundreds of them in our own camp, and it was also a lot of Bosniak males jailed in two of the schools in Vares. And this led to -- that the Bosniaks started an assault for the whole town of Vares, and that's why I talked and negotiated with the operational group in Dabravine, because they said now the Croat have made this and now we will kill them, we will destroy the town of Vares. And I managed to convince them that it was better to take it a little easier to check what has happened and let me come into the village of Stupni Do and check the situation and to be a link between the operational group and the Croats to avoid more bloodshed. And we managed with that for some days. Maybe it also made the Bosniaks -- created some calm period for them to make preparations. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: With this come any different units now to Vares? Did you see the emergence of another unit in Vares then?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: I didn't see any other military units in Vares until on the 4th of November -- okay, we saw during this chaotic period some other military -- or not units but the individuals, Serbian officers going into the Bobovac Brigade headquarters and so on. But really units I saw in Vares, the town of Vares, for the first time on the morning of 4th of November.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Can you inform the Trial Chamber as to which unit this was and from which army.

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Yes. And the reason I met them and not my unit was that I had at that time got reinforcement from FrenchBat but I was down to meet the company and the company commander in the southern part of Vares. And there were no Frenchmen but there was a Bosniak unit and they didn't look very confident, so I stopped and talked with them and asked, "Who is the commander?" And one man asked -- answered without hesitation and said, "That's me." And then I asked from where he came, and he said, "We are from the 7th Muslim Brigade." And then we had a short conversation. I told them a little what -- about what had happened prior in Vares, and then I told him now to consider his responsibility and be a good example and avoid what has been done by the Croats and keep up to national and humanitarian laws. And he said yes. And then I left further south to find the French company.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did you observe then if your instructions were carried out?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Well, as I said, I just passed on out of the town. But when I came back some hours later, I really realised he didn't care the least about what I said or at least couldn't control it, because then the looting and impedement in Vares was under full swing.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Would you say then that the situation worsened? Would I be correct if you said that the situation worsened --

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Yes, of course --

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: -- on your return?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Yes. It was chaotic and out of control. It was a lot of firing in the air and screaming and looting in the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you describe the physical condition of the town for us, please, the buildings, how they looked to you and ...

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Well, at that time -- well, the town is partly old and partly some higher buildings built somewhere in the 1960s, 1970s. And some of the buildings were burnt by the Croats some days earlier and also some looting took place then. But now it was chaotic and a lot of windows was smashed and the soldiers stole what they could find. They also stole some cars, tried to steal others. They also went into the food storage of the units' yard and were all over the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And when you say "the soldiers," could you tell the Trial Chamber which unit you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Well, I thought then and I still thought it was from the 7th Muslim Brigade. I didn't saw any signs on some other units up there. And in my talks with the operational group in Dabravine - because I went back there when I saw what was on in Vares, because what happened there was a responsibility for my company commander - so I went back to the operational group and told them to take control over the situation, and he said, "Yes, we will," and they sent a unit of military police and they came. They were not too many, but they tried. So -- and they -- the day ended up with some of the Bosniak soldiers lying dead on the streets that day, shot by their own military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Brigadier General, from the period of September 1993 and perhaps until the end of November 1994 [sic], what is your opinion of what transpired in the Vares area? How would you best describe it?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Well, it was, of course, a fight to control the important strategic road up to Northern Bosnia. That was one part of it. And it was not just militarily strategic; it was economically strategic, because the parties also took tolls from all transportation going up there. It was a lot of checkpoints where normal people had to pay to come through. It was also an important area for the black market and smuggling in that area. So it was both militarily important but it was also important for the -- call it organised crime, or what you will call it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I'd like to correct the transcript I think in line 12, paragraph -- page 21. It says "end of November 1994" and that should be end of November 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Other than the economic situation and the military situation, from a civilian point of view was this area a tense area at that time? Was it, you know, could you elaborate for us, please.

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Yes. The civilian situation was -- as I said before, it was a Croat majority in the town, and due to what happened and the Croat extremists, first they threatened their own people that if they didn't leave Vares when the extremists left or -- I think it was around the 2nd, it was the 2nd and the 3rd of November mainly -- they would be killed by the Bosniaks. And a lot of people - hundreds, maybe a thousand of them - left. And then when the Bosniaks took control over Vares, the majority changed, so a lot of Muslims or Bosniaks moved into the town. So after and in the middle of November and so on it became a Bosniak majority in the town and the mayor became a Bosniak and the brigade or the defence there were -- became a Bosniak task.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And at that point in time, would you say that Vares then became calm?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Yes, compared with the situation before. Yes, it became stable at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I believe that one of your duties, as you outlined before, was to try to make as much peace as you could have between the parties. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And I think you may have set out in your duties to try to demilitarise, if for a better word, the town, so to speak. Were you able to achieve this?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: We did not. But -- and the idea was that we should took over the security and defence of the town from the parties, but they were not very interested in that. We made that proposal and we asked -- I think it was on the 5th of November or something like that -- the 2nd Corps and mayor of Tuzla to come down and to talk about this and to negotiate. They also wanted us to be some buffer zone between the 2nd and the 3rd Corps, which we turned down because we were not interested in that. It was not our task to be a buffer. So it went out of nothing and the parties was not interested, and of course the Vares area get under Bosniak control. And that was -- I can understand that they prefer that solution, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Brigadier General.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this concludes the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Benjamin. You were very expeditious, as you only used half an hour. I turn now to the Defence to give them the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General Henricsson. My name is Edina Residovic, and I represent General Hadzihasanovic. Allow me to ask you a few questions. You told us that as the commander of the Nordic Battalion you were in Bosnia and Herzegovina from September the 1st, 1993 until the 6th of April in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the war had been ongoing for almost a year and a half; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were aware of the fact that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was the legitimate armed force of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During your tour of duty, you learnt quite a lot about the 2nd Corps and your knowledge about the 2nd Corps was far better than your knowledge of the structure, responsibilities, and missions of the other corps of the BH army; would I be right in putting it that way?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, as you have already testified, in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps and within the ABiH there were several HVO brigades that accepted the command of the 2nd Corps and of the ABiH army in accordance with the laws of the country of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, General, that other HVO units, and particularly in the area of Herzegovina and in Central Bosnia, waged an armed struggle against the ABiH army and -- while you were there, especially along the Neretva River Valley, the town of Mostar, Jablanica, Konjic, and in the Lasva Valley? Were you aware of these facts?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have already said, General, that the only road linking the areas of the 1st, 6th, 3rd, and 2nd Corps was the road leading through Vares. That is why, as you yourself said, from the standpoint of the civilian population, as well as in military terms, this was an area of extreme strategic significance, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If this route was obstructed or if it were to be gained control of by enemy forces, that is, the HVO or the Army of Republika Srpska, the North and North-Eastern Bosnia would be totally cut off from the rest of the country and would find themselves in an extremely difficult situation; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time already you knew that the Croatian Defence Council, and in particular its command in Grude, Vitez, and Kiseljak, was cooperating with the VRS in the fighting against the ABiH and this was particularly obvious earlier, when the attack occurred on Travnik, Bugojno, Zepce, and you were also able to see officers of the VRS in Vares, where the HVO Bobovac Brigade was stationed. Were you aware of these facts?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: I was not aware of the cooperation with the Defence -- the Croatian Defence Council. I learned that later. But it's right that I saw Serbian officers coming into the headquarters of the Bobovac Brigade after Ivica Rajic took it over. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, from the military standpoint, isn't it quite normal for the ABiH to be concerned by the fact that the Bobovac Brigade, and especially the fresh forces that arrived in Vares, were refusing to succumb to the command of the 2nd Corps and were being resubordinated to the command in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You believe that it was normal that several corps cooperated and prepared a plan to take over Vares as an important strategic location linking the forces of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Yes. During these conditions, it was like normal. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time or later you probably learnt that the operation to gain control of Vares was carried out in cooperation by three corps.

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: At that time, I was not aware about three corps. My picture -- okay, the 1st Corps was involved, but I didn't know about the 2nd Corps at that time, because I thought it was 3 Corps and 2nd Corps and partly 1st Corps, the one I met in Dabravine, the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: A witness has appeared in this courtroom, Mr. Birger Hakan, who describing the events that occurred prior to this claimed that the attack of the army units on Kopjari was a very well-executed combat operation in military terms and that after accusations made by the HVO that a crime had been committed in Kopjari, there was an investigation by the international forces which did not produce any evidence of a crime having been committed in this village. Would you agree with this statement given before this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Yes. Major Birger was the one who was in Kopjari. I was not. So I have full trust in his report.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have testified to the effect that on the 23rd of October you learnt from members of the ABiH that Stupni Do had been attacked. This is a village not far from Vares inhabited by Bosnian Muslims. Did you learn of that?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Yes. I learnt that from the 1st Corps or the operational group in Dabravine, but on the 23rd they were not quite sure of what had happened. It was more or less a rumour at that time. And that's why I, as I said before, negotiated with them to -- and promised to check what exactly had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After receiving this information, you demanded from the HVO command that you be allowed access to Stupni Do, and in spite of repeated requests it was not granted; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From a distance of about a kilometre and a half you observed Stupni Do and you saw that the village was on fire; but because of the smoke and the distance, you couldn't really see what was happening in the village, could you?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your units shortly after that met refugees fleeing from Stupni Do and Major Egberg informed you that the refugees were in a state of shock, that they couldn't speak, with the exception of two young women, who told them that there was burning, looting, and raping in Stupni Do and that they too, these two 20-year-old young women, had been raped. Is that what you were told?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Regarding the HVO behaviour, you informed their command in Kiseljak about this, and after repeated interventions you managed on the 26th of October to enter Stupni Do; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you had other obligations, you didn't stay long in Stupni Do but you took a walk around. You saw that the houses were totally or partially burnt. You saw dead bodies, burnt corpses, but detailed information about the village was collected later by members of your battalion and of the British Battalion, who came to assist you in securing the village. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You entered the village even though the Bobovac HVO Brigade tried to prevent you from doing that by force. They opened fire on your battalion. They set mines, but you managed to remove them and that is how you were able to be a witness of the crime that happened in this village. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the 2nd of November, you learnt that the HVO Bobovac Brigade had left Vares, taking with it a part of the population. But you were also able to see that the HVO was forcing a part of the Croat population to leave this area. They were exerting pressure on them to leave the area.

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: There were still HVO units or soldiers in Vares on the 3rd, the beginning of the 3rd of November, and I never saw the HVO units exerting pressure. It was reported to me, but I didn't see it personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In answering a question from my learned friend, your soldiers also saw that while withdrawing the HVO were setting fire to its own property, some of the houses that were damaged in Vares and the surroundings, the damage was due to what they did upon pulling out. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After the takeover of Vares by members of the ABiH, you learnt that the HVO was withdrawing across territories under the control of the VRS, which for you was evidence that these two armies had already reached agreement on cooperation; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: That they withdrew over VRS territory was completely true. That doesn't prove that the cooperation was on the high command. For me at the time, I was not surprise forward there was more or less private negotiation on the low level, but -- so it doesn't prove for me that the cooperation was on a high level.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I wonder whether the other Defence team have any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. On behalf of Mr. Kubura's team, we will have a few questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, can we go back to the 4th of November when you arrived in Vares and when you said that you noticed members at 7th Brigade there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You recognised them because their commander introduced himself as being the commander of the 7th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Yes. And they also wore the badge of that brigade, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, when talking to my learned friends from the Prosecution, you said that the total number of soldiers was about 80; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Yes. On that spot, when I first met them, it was around that. I can't tell you exactly, but that's how I remember it today. But you must also know that the area and the terrain there was rather difficult to overview.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters correction: It was not from the Prosecution. "When talking to my friends," said the counsel. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there's an error in the transcript. In line 13 I meant that the witness spoke to my colleague from the Defence team, not from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: At that point in time, the situation in town was peaceful, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that. It was definitely not peaceful, at least not when that unit -- those units arrived. It was more -- better to describe as chaotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And after Vares, you went to Dabravine a few hours later. That is my understanding. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Well, immediately after my meeting with this unit, I went directly down south to meet the French company. And after some hours, I went - maybe one hour - I went back up to Vares and then the situation was out of control. And when I saw that, I went down to the operational group in Dabravine and asked them to take control of the situation in Vares and to -- and in my, as I then experienced it, the operational group was not in command of the units in Vares. I thought it was the 3rd Corps. But I asked them to communicate with the commanders and the officer under control of Vares to take his units under control. And they then sent a military police unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You just mentioned units, and that brings me to my next question. When you returned to Vares from Dabravine, you found many more soldiers than the 80 that you mentioned as being members of the 7th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that in the town of Vares itself, in addition to members of the 7th Brigade, there were also the members of the 126th and 110th Brigades and soldiers of the municipal TO of Vares, I hope you will agree with me.

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: I can't do that. I can't say that everybody came from the 7th Brigade, but I can't say that they came from the unit you mentioned. It could have been all from 7th Brigade; they can also have been from different units, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned the UNHCR warehouse that soldiers apparently entered. Members of your battalion were securing that warehouse, weren't they? Of your Nordic Battalion.

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: They took over the protection of it, but at that time they -- the ABiH soldiers already were in there, so we had to get them out of the storage.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: During the events in Vares, you compiled reports which you forwarded on. Did you send them to the 3rd Corps or another superior command of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Well, I informed first, as I said, I had -- I communicated with the operational group in Dabravine. I communicated with the 2nd Corps. And then I communicated, of course, with my superior commander, General Briquemont, and his staff in Kiseljak. And the link to the 3rd Corps went through Bosnia-Herzegovina command or through the 1st Operational Group in the ABiH, and of course - I hope at least - that the 2nd and 3rd Corps could talk with each other. But I didn't negotiate or meet with officers or a commander of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the operative group that you had contact with in Dabravine was not a member of the 7th Brigade or an officer of the 7th Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we have the re-examination and the questions by the Judges, it would be better to have the break. It is 10.25. And we will resume at five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is now time for re-examination. Ms. Benjamin, do you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecution -- Mr. President, the Prosecution doesn't have any re-examination at this time. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges have some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, the Judges sitting before you have a number of questions for you in order to clarify some of the answers you provided to the questions put to you by both parties, and in order to fill in certain gaps. It is necessary to do this -- it is necessary to clarify these matters in order to be quite clear and in the interest of justice. General, first of all, I would like to ask you: When you were in Vares, how long were you there for? What was the exact period of time that you spent there? Could you specify the dates.

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Well, for this period, I arrived to Vares on the 23rd of October, and I stayed there until the 25th. Then I -- sorry, I -- yes -- no, I stayed until late 24th. I was then in Zvornik negotiating with the Serbs on the 25th, and on the 25th in the evening when violations started in Vares I went back and was there, when from the late evening 25th until the 28th, I think - 28th, yes - I passed through Vares on the 29th, and then I went back to Vares on the 3rd of November and stayed there until the 5th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you say that you were in Vares from the 3rd to the 5th. Where did you stay? Because between the 3rd and the 5th, it was the night from -- between the 3rd and the 4th and the 4th and the 5th. Where did you stay during this period?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: I stayed at the camp of my 8th Company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And the camp of the 8th Company, how far was it from the centre of the town?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Well, it was 2 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2 kilometres. During the two days that you spent there, the 3rd, the 4th, and the 5th, did you meet any foreigners apart from the mayor? Any foreigners such as European Union representatives?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm quite sure I did, but I cannot tell you exactly. I don't remember that, which people I met. But we have a continuous communication with the BH command, with the United Nations military observers, with the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The ECMM monitors, did you speak to them over the phone or did you meet them in order to discuss the subject of the town of Vares?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: If I talked with them, then I met them. I had no talks with them over the phone, as I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when you spoke to them, did you talk about the situation which you described as being chaotic? Was this something that you talked about with them?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: I don't remember that, because that was mainly a task for my company commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But your company commander was under your authority.

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the commander of the 8th Company could replace you when speaking to European Union monitors.

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: He could replace me if he followed the guidelines he had, and I think that's quite normal. But if I were on the spot and we had communication with the ECMM, I think I should have attended it. But I don't recall that in my memory today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In response to a question put to you, you said that in the depot of the high commission there were problems. There were problems with a certain depot. And you said that it was necessary to leave -- to take soldiers out of the depots, BH soldiers had to be taken out of these depots. Who guarded these depots?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly the position of my own company down here. As I said, that was part of the company, the commander's responsibility, and of course mine at the whole. But when the looting started in Vares - and I say -- can tell you when you have -- I think we had about 150 operative men in Vares - then a town of 50.000 people are very big, so you can't be all over the place. But I myself came down to the storage during the 4th with my command APC, and that's when I saw that the BiH soldiers has gone into the storage. And together with some of my soldiers on the spot we took over, blocked the door with APC, and took them out of the storage, and closed the gates and took over the guarding of the storage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you used legitimate force in order to deal with the way in which these soldiers were conducting themselves.

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Yes. We -- well, legitimate force? We used robust action to get them out. We didn't use weapons or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But you didn't use your weapons. Why do you say that these soldiers were BH soldiers? How many people were in these storage facilities? Were they in uniform? Did they have any insignia on them? Did they have any weapons? Were they in combat gear? Could you describe them for us.

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: They were definitely in combat gear. They had weapons. They had uniforms. I didn't notice any badges, signs on them in -- at that moment. They were rather aggressive, and I think we were lucky we had better quality soldiers. We had more equipment and armoured personnel carriers, so we were superior to them. And I think they realised it was not a good idea to stay in the storage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why do you say that they were soldiers rather than bandits or people who were engaged in looting? Why are you persuaded that these people were soldiers, that is to say that they were part of an organised structure? What are the grounds for making such a claim?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: They wore uniforms. They were armed. They also had a bus outside the storage at that time with -- and altogether could have been around 50 persons, 50 soldier, around there. And -- but sometimes I can admit it was not so easy to separate crooks, bandits, from the soldiers, because I would say that the respect for international humanitarian laws and the discipline in the units was not very impressive to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 50 individuals you have described as soldiers, was there some sort of an officer structure there? Were these officers from the base, or did you think -- were these basic officers or did you think there were middle-ranking officers among them?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: I think there were. I think there were, but I couldn't see it. Because they were out of control, as I saw it. Maybe they had the task to rob that storage. But I didn't see any officer trying to get control of the unit and making them follow the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This peaceful confrontation you had with them, since weapons weren't used, how long did it last? How long did it take before you could take control of the situation and make them leave? As far as you can remember, how much time did this take?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Well first, I wouldn't describe it as peaceful, but it was without weapons used. And just at the storage, until we gained control of it, I think it might have lasted 15 minutes before I left the place and gave the command over to my -- to the unit on the spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is something that happened a long time ago. But do you remember whether these soldiers had walkie-talkies or any communications equipment? Because as you are a professional military officer, you know that units in the field always have means of communication. Do you remember seeing any such equipment?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: I don't remember that, but I can say that devices of communication, radio equipment, was very rare in the Bosnian army at that time, so even on platoon and company level they lacked radios. And I know that very well because they stole from us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are telling us that the battalion -- that BritBat and other battalions had equipment stolen from them.

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In response to one of the questions put to you, you said that you went to the operational group in order to ask them to put an end to such behaviour. You said that in the operational group you met the commander, the person who was in charge. Do you remember the name of this commander or not?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you gave him an account of what you had seen and when you told him about the looting carried out by these individuals who might be described as soldiers, what impression did he give you? Since you said that he sent the military police there. If these were bandits, highway bandits, he should have told you, "Take this up with the municipality or the civilian police." Why in such a case would he have sent the military police there? Could you provide us with some clarifications about this very precise situation.

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Yes. I think he was very well aware that it was units from BiH in the town, and he never denied that and said anything that it's not my business. He listened seriously to what I said, and he said, "We will do something against this." And they did obviously, because they sent military police. But I never saw him there. I never saw -- and on the 4th of November I spent a lot of time down in the town of Vares, and I never saw any officers doing any obvious attempt to get control of the situation. But I saw, as I said earlier, the military police. They tried to stop it, and they even fired live on their own soldiers, and I think we had two or three dead on the streets during that day. And that, I think, shows that discipline was not very impressive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, I was going to ask you this question, but you've already answered it. In line 6, page 23 you said -- and in line 4, you said that the military police opened fire on the soldiers. Was this an event that you were informed about? Do you have hearsay information about it? Or were you a witness of this event? Did you see the military police using their weapons against other soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: I did. And that was a specific situation when they fired at a car which didn't stop for a stopping sign which was made by the police, the military police. They didn't stop and the car ran away and they fired at it and they hit it. But it didn't stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was the car a civilian one or a military one?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: It was a civilian car with soldiers in it, a stolen one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a stolen car. The people who were killed, why do you say that they were soldiers, since you are telling us that they were in a civilian vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: They wore uniforms. And I would say that there were very, very few civilians out during these days because of the danger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many people were killed in this event?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: As I said, I saw two bodies on the street personally, and I don't remember what our reports said afterwards. And so -- two people at least. That's what I can say with security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apart from the 8th Battalion, it seems that a French unit was also present. Who else was present in the field?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: You mean the 8th Company. But on the 4th, it arrived a French company from the foreign legionnaires. But they came late that day and was not operative until the next day, on the 5th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be operational when you're part of a foreign unit, when your in a foreign country, what does that consist of? Does it mean having a physical presence in the street, an armed physical presence in the street? Does it mean that one is involved in protecting facilities, buildings such as storage facilities? What exactly does it mean when one is present in such a chaotic situation? How did you attempt to resolve this problem?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: Well, as I remember it, the company was operational or in that way on the 5th, that they protected -- I think it was because the 8th Company at that time was very tired; they had been in full swing for more or less a week the day around. So they released our checkpoints, I know at the church, the Catholic church, to protect it. I think they also took over the storage for UNHCR. And that was a rather easy task for trained, skilled soldiers, which this company consisted of. So they were doing their job on the 5th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you left the area, was the situation stable or was the situation identical to the one that prevailed on the 4th?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: No. Late on the 5th the situation was stable, for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as far as you are aware, was there Croatian civilian population that had remained in the town in spite of the fact that many had left? Were there still Croats in the town?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: It was still Croats in the town. That's my impression. The number I can't tell you, but there were people staying all the time and still is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And these people weren't particularly concerned, weren't particularly worried about anything? Had they requested protection of any kind? What sort of relationship did you have with this Croatian population?

utterances.speaker: ULF HENRICSSON
utterances.text: We had a good relation with all civilians in Vares, and at this time the Croats wanted protection, and we did whatever we could to do that, as we did when the Croats impeded the Bosniaks. That was why we were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We don't have any further questions either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And the same for the Prosecution, Mr. President. We have no questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, as you have probably realised, this completes your examination because the parties have no further questions for you, nor do the Judges. We would like to thank you for having come to The Hague to testify about what happened during the mission you were involved in in this part of Bosnia and Herzegovina in September, October, November of 1993. We would like to thank you for your contribution to establishing the truth, and we would like to wish you a good trip home. And naturally we wish you all the best in your current profession in this military college. I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, I will give you the floor, but before I do so I just wanted to clarify a minor matter that concerns the fact that the Trial Chamber, after having heard what your position is, plans to call a number of witnesses. You asked whether these witnesses should appear before the Prosecution concludes its case or after, and you mentioned Rule 98 bis. In order to clarify this issue, the Trial Chamber intends to call proprio motu nine witnesses before the end of the Prosecution's case. So as I said, that would be before. Because according to the Rules of Procedure, according to Rule 85, the Prosecution presents its evidence and it is within that framework that the witnesses called by the Trial Chamber appear. It is only afterwards, after the presentation of the Prosecution's case, that Rule 98 bis or the provisions covered by Rule 98 bis are applicable. So that is how we will be proceeding. Mr. Mundis, you may take the floor now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution has no further witnesses scheduled for today. The witness who is scheduled for tomorrow will be made available first thing in the morning. I did want to say, however, that perhaps, if it would be helpful, and given the fact that we do have a substantial period of time left today, if I could suggest the following: In light of and having had the opportunity over the break to review the nine witnesses that the Trial Chamber was interested in having called, the Prosecution would be in a position to present its views with respect to those nine witnesses; however, I do need to make a couple of inquiries with respect to two or three of those witnesses. I believe that if I were to have a recess now of approximately 45 minutes, I would then be in a position to at least elaborate on the Prosecution's view with respect to those nine witnesses at that time. I hesitate to add this, Mr. President, but I -- with respect to what I said previously about the interaction between Rule 85 and Rule 98 bis, I would like to discuss this issue also with my colleagues from the Defence for both accused. But for now the Prosecution would respectfully reserve its right to revisit or to -- revisit the entire issue of the interaction between Rules 98, 85, and 98 bis. But perhaps we can further address that after I've had an opportunity to discuss the issue with my colleagues from the Defence. So perhaps, Mr. President, if you'd like to hear the Prosecution views at least with respect to the nine witnesses, I believe we'd be prepared to address Your Honours at about 12.15 on that issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber raised a moment ago the question of the witness for Friday and the question of the video. I wish to draw the attention of the Prosecution to this issue once again. There are a certain number of videotapes which are listed on your list; and as you know, before making a final ruling on all of these documents and exhibits, has asked the Prosecution to carry out a number of measures. Regarding the videos, and especially the video that could be tendered through the witness on Friday, I am inviting the Prosecution to make a selection among those videos and to consider the video for which there is a transcript, number 00818539. And if this transcript comes from a video, it would be desirable and in the interest of justice that the video - especially if it's not too long - for the video to be broadcast, and afterwards the witness can be examined about it. On the other hand, there is another video about the Mujahedin, but that is a separate problem. But there is a video which appears to correspond fully to the witness that will appear on Friday. So can you please consider the matter closely so as to avoid that after hearing the witness we are forced to make him come again, because we feel that the video certainly should be publicly broadcast. You asked for 45 minutes, and we will resume about quarter past 12.00 or twenty past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed, with a few minutes' delay. But before giving the floor to both parties, the Chamber would like to situate the problem emanating from the issues we raised a moment ago in a more general framework, which is the following. Some time ago the Prosecution asked us to admit into evidence hundreds of documents. Following this request, the Defence made their observations on the grounds that some of those documents could be produced in the presence of a witness. Following that, the Prosecution notified us that they intended to withdraw 19 witnesses, and they did so several days ago, from a list of witnesses which was determined by the Chamber in accordance with Rule 73 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The Prosecution is requesting the withdrawal of those witnesses, without providing us any explanations regarding the motives that have prompted them to withdraw those witnesses, whereas those witnesses were envisaged when the Chamber determined the number of witnesses and the duration of the hearings. The Chamber notes that among the withdrawn witnesses a certain number could authenticate certain documents which are still outstanding and that in order to respond to the concern of the Prosecution regarding the admission of its documents and also those of the Defence which requires that some documents be authenticated by witnesses, one might consider calling a certain number of witnesses in the weeks that will come before the closing of the Prosecution case, and the Chamber has selected nine such witnesses. So the Chamber wanted to tell you this because these witnesses had already been scheduled. They are not additional witnesses. They are not witnesses coming in support of additional evidence. These were witnesses who had been scheduled and who could assist in the authentification of documents. That is how the Chamber sees the problem at this stage. Judge Swart would like to add something as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: The question that is put before us by your communication of Monday is the following: Was it a wise decision to eliminate 19 witnesses and would you be prepared to reconsider it, notably with respect to 9 witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and Your Honours, for the opportunity to address you. Let me start -- perhaps before getting to Judge Swart's question, let me attempt to provide a little bit of background for the benefit of the Trial Chamber and the Defence with respect to the prosecution of this case as it concerned the duty of the accused to punish the perpetrators of the crimes for -- which the indictment is concerned with. The pre-trial filings of the Prosecution, including its pre-trial brief and through the opening statement of the Prosecution in this case, to a certain extent, Your Honours, has been overtaken by some of the evidence which has been adduced. That is, when we commenced the trial and filed our pre-trial Rule 65 ter package including the list of witnesses, there were certain elements, if you will, that the Prosecution was attempting to establish from numerous angles, to use a colloquial phrase, it was a "belt and suspenders approach." Largely as a result of evidence that was adduced by the Defence during the course of the cross-examination of the expert General Reinhardt, the Prosecution's views with respect to the actual steps taken by the accused and in light of General Reinhardt's report, we would submit that the issues that are involved in this case have been substantially narrowed; that is, we are of the view that the duty of the commander in the ABiH was to investigate and refer cases to the district military courts. Our view is that the court prosecutors and court judges would only be able to add a limited amount of evidence, if any, to the actual issues that are now being Your Honours.
