That is, whereas prior to trial we were attempting to demonstrate steps taken at the trial level in the district military courts through calling prosecutors or judges from both district military courts and the functioning civilian courts, our view is now such that because it's clear that the obligation of the commanders was to investigate and refer these witnesses are not necessarily as probative as they otherwise appeared to the Prosecution to be when we commenced our trial. In addition, Mr. President, the Prosecution in reviewing these legal witnesses, for lack of a better term, that would cover seven of the nine witnesses that Your Honours have specifically addressed, the Prosecution has had some difficulties with respect to some of these witnesses, as reflected in the testimony of some of the witnesses who have appeared as well as some of the witnesses who have yet to appear, in the sense that they do not necessarily advance the Prosecution case in a manner in which the Prosecution would put them before this Trial Chamber as being of -- or as having probative information or evidence for the value of the Trial Chamber. Those are some general comments. With respect to -- or to provide you with a couple of examples, Mr. President, I would ask to do that in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, let us go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with respect to the witness number 77, Jason Medley, Mr. Medley is currently serving in the British Army. He's stationed at the British Embassy in Washington, DC. We made a determination that Mr. Medley's testimony would be largely cumulative with respect to other British soldiers who have testified and the combination of the cumulative nature of Mr. Medley's testimony, plus the fact that we anticipated that his testimony in chief would last some 45 minutes, it was a simple question of economics that we determined that the costs to the Tribunal of bringing Mr. Medley here for such limited testimony was not necessary under the circumstances, as the Office of the Prosecutor determined them. And I think, Mr. President, that really summarises the Prosecution position with respect to these nine witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I still am at a loss a little bit to know in what way your case has now changed. You say as a result of the hearing to have witness Reinhardt, as a result of the material produced by Defence, we have a different view of our case. The question is: What has remained and what has gone? You have said a few things in general, but I have difficulty in getting your point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly. I wanted to intervene on this point. But let us go back into private session, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, after the question that was raised yesterday, Defence counsel has considered the suggestions that you made, but in accordance with the schedule that you announced, we thought that perhaps the Prosecution and Defence counsel would present their positions tomorrow. But given the current situation, our position can't be expressed quite precisely in relation to all the very important issues raised today. The position of the Defence is that we must at all times bear in mind the basic principle -- the fundamental principle involved in all criminal proceedings, namely the rights of the accused. This primarily concerns the accused's right to respond to everything presented by the Prosecution before this Trial Chamber, and it also concerns the main obligation of the Prosecution, which is to prove its case. After the comments made by my learned colleague, the Defence is not quite certain, because we haven't -- about the position to adopt, because we haven't seen an amended indictment, given that the indictment mentioned a very broad form of responsibility, command responsibility, according to which the accused didn't take certain measures in order to punish and prevent. For these reasons - and naturally I'm bearing in mind the rights of the accused and I'm also applying the Rules of this Tribunal - the Trial Chamber after the conclusion of the Prosecution's case should take one of the decisions provided for by the Rules of the Tribunal. The Defence has the right to proceed in this manner. This has been pointed out by my learned colleagues. In such a case, our position would be that the Trial Chamber should state whether it considers that the Prosecution has been able to prove its case. On the other hand, although we tried to discover what the jurisprudence of this Tribunal was with regard to this matter, with the exception of one case that hasn't been concluded yet before the Appeals Chamber - the case is still pending - so apart from this case, we haven't encountered a similar situation in which the Trial Chamber called witnesses while one of the parties was still presenting its case before the Chamber. Some of the witnesses included in the list were potential Defence witnesses, so they could be called when the Defence commences with the presentation of its case. For these reasons and given that the Trial Chamber, as you Mr. President have said, has the right to order that a party present certain evidence at any point in time, or given that the Trial Chamber can call witnesses if this is in the interest of justice, and given that we are not sure whether the Trial Chamber will do this at the end of the presentation of the evidence or at the end of the presentation of the evidence by one of the cases, and given that we believe that any decision, either to have the evidence presented or to have the Trial Chamber call this witness -- these witnesses, we believe that regardless of the decision taken, the rights of the accused -- the interests of the accused should be taken into account. As well -- and we also think that the Prosecution has the duty to prove its case. We don't have a final position with regard to this matter, so we would like the Trial Chamber to consider the arguments presented by our learned colleagues from the Prosecution and to take into consideration our positions. And we would like the Trial Chamber to reach a decision and when doing so to bear in mind the rights of the accused. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I only have one point to add, and that being of course we respect the right of the Prosecution to put its case in the way that it sees best and to call the evidence that supports such a case. At the same time, Your Honours, according to the Rules, do have the discretionary power, of course, to order the parties to call witnesses or to call witnesses Your Honours' selves in order to safeguard the interests of justice. The only question - and this is the point that I do wish to make - is when that should occur; whether it should occur at a point during the case of either of the parties, after their case, or at the end of the case. In this particular situation, Your Honours, we don't have any submissions at this stage on what would be the best time for that to occur. It's, of course, a matter for Your Honours to consider. And as Your Honours have indicated, it is closely related to the documents and the authentication of those documents. It may be, because it relates to documents the Prosecution seeks to rely upon, that it is for the Prosecution to call those witnesses in order that that evidence be made part of the Prosecution case, evidence that the Prosecution would then rely upon, but that is a matter for Your Honours. It could be that those witnesses are done independently. But in our submission, it may be, as it is part to have Prosecution case, the best way for it for the Prosecution to be ordered to call those witnesses if they are for the purposes of authenticating their documents. I'm grateful, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: May I ask Mr. Mundis two questions in this respect regarding to what Mr. Dixon has said and our Presiding Judge in the beginning. In our view, there is a discussion of having witnesses in court related to the issue of admitting documents. The Defence has expressed a very strong desire, a very clear design repeatedly to have admitted evidence by means of a witness. If you are going to reduce your list with 19 witnesses, this is going to be more difficult. So we would like to hear your opinion on that, not necessarily now but maybe tomorrow. The second thing that I have been asking myself since last Monday is the following: If you are reducing your list with 19 witnesses, that more or less amounts to a very rigorous amendment of your list. And from what you have done so far or your predecessor, Mr. Withopf, I conclude that you are of the opinion that you are completely free to use your list of witnesses or not to use your list of witnesses completely. That is for you and for nobody else to decide whether a witness will in effect be called or not. Is that a proper summary of your position in this respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Judge Swart, Your Honour, let me start with the first question. In terms of the need for witnesses to authenticate the documents, the Prosecution would submit that the nine witnesses that have been discussed here this morning I don't believe would be the proper witnesses to authenticate more than perhaps only a handful of the hundred of contested documents anyway. I'm a bit at a loss to understand the specific link between these nine witnesses and authentication of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Well, you have, for instance, submitted documents for admission concerning the Zenica and the Travnik court registrars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes. Clearly, Your Honour, there are a few documents that could be authenticated by these witnesses, but the vast majority of the documents would not fall into that category, I would submit. Let me perhaps come back to that question tomorrow. With respect to the second question, it has certainly been my recollection of practice, both before this Trial Chamber and before other Trial Chambers, that either of the parties may withdraw witnesses or simply not call such witnesses upon due notice to the Chamber and the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Defence. We have on a number of occasions, as Your Honours and my learned colleagues are aware, dropped or not called witnesses at various points throughout this trial for a number of reasons. The Prosecution would submit that it is in fact primarily for the parties to determine which witnesses to call and the precise -- one of the precise reasons why Rule 98 is in the Rules, permits Judges to call those witnesses that they want to hear, whether those witnesses were originally on the Prosecution or Defence list or any other witness that the Trial Chamber thinks would be helpful. And again, the Prosecution would submit that Rule 85 sets forth a default order in the presentation of witnesses, if you will, so that those witnesses are heard at the end of the trial. But it is generally speaking our view that it is for the Prosecution to determine which witnesses to call in its case, just as it is for the Defence to determine which witnesses they want to call in their case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to know your position on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber has taken note of what the Prosecution has said, and we have also taken note of the Defence counsel's position in relation to the issue of withdrawing witnesses. And as I already said this morning, we'll deliberate after having listened to what both parties have said and we will then render our decision concerning the 19 witnesses -- unless the Defence wants to make submissions up until tomorrow, because we were informed that the Defence would like to reflect on the matter -- But given that withdrawing Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. witnesses can only be satisfactory from the point of view of the Defence, I don't know what the Defence could add. Mrs. Residovic, would you like some time to provide us with additional arguments tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't think we need to make any additional submissions tomorrow, and this is why we leave it to the Trial Chamber to reach a decision about this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I thought you meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes. I fully concur with Ms. Residovic on this point. There's no further submission that we need to make on this matter, which primarily concerns the Prosecution and Your Honours' exercise of Your Honours' discretion. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It's almost time to adjourn. We have about another ten minutes left. Are there any other issues to raise? If not -- I see that Mr. Bourgon is remaining very silent. There are no other submissions to be made. Mr. Mundis has nothing to say either. As that is the case, we will now adjourn and I will see everyone tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 20th day of May, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.24 p.m.,
